title: Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District
body:
The Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District collects and treats the valley's sewage. It serves the City of Santa Clarita and the unincorporated areas around it, Stevenson Ranch and Castaic among them, about 250,000 residents and businesses, through more than 42 miles of trunk sewers, one pumping plant and two treatment plants, the Saugus and Valencia water reclamation plants.[1] The local sewers that feed its trunk lines are the City's or the County's.[1] It is one of the 24 districts of the Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, formed under the County Sanitation District Act of 1923, which share one staff at Whittier under a joint administration agreement while each keeps its own board. Its board is the Mayor of Santa Clarita, a second member of the City Council, and the chair of the County Board of Supervisors.[1]

The Saugus plant, on Springbrook Avenue, began operating in 1962. It was enlarged in 1964, 1965 and 1968, given tertiary filters in 1987, and brought to its design capacity of 6.5 million gallons a day in 1991; it handles no solids, which go by trunk sewer to Valencia.[2] The Valencia plant, on 27 acres on The Old Road west of Interstate 5, opened in 1967 with a capacity of 1.5 million gallons a day and was enlarged to 21.6 million by 2003. It processes the solids from both plants.[3]

The district is the union of two older ones. District No. 26, formed in 1962, served the eastern half of the valley from the Saugus plant; District No. 32, formed in 1965, served the western half from Valencia. When the east's sewage outgrew the Saugus plant, which its site would not let it enlarge, a pipeline carried the excess to Valencia, and in 1984 the two districts signed an agreement to share the system and its costs. They were consolidated as the Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District in 2005.[1]

The plants discharge treated water to the Santa Clara River under permits with chloride limits. The Regional Water Quality Control Board set an objective of 100 milligrams per liter for the river, to protect salt-sensitive crops downstream, and the plants do not remove chloride.[4][5] The district went first after household water softeners: voters approved Measure S on November 4, 2008, enacting the Santa Clara River Chloride Reduction Ordinance of 2008, which required residential automatic water softeners to be removed by June 30, 2009. More than 8,000 were taken out, but the plants still could not meet the limit.[4][6] In October 2013 the board approved a chloride compliance project and certified its environmental impact report. A court set the report aside in 2016; the board certified a recirculated report on August 30, 2017, and the litigation over it ended in February 2022.[5] Ultraviolet disinfection began at both plants in 2021, and an advanced treatment plant using reverse osmosis at Valencia in October 2023, its brine trucked to the Districts' plant in Carson.[5][3]
footnotes: Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Who We Are & What We Do For You," https://www.lacsd.org/services/wastewater-programs-permits/wastewater-revenue-program/who-we-are-what-we-do-for-you, as captured by the Internet Archive on 19 May 2026: "The Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District (SCVSD) primarily serves the City of Santa Clarita and the surrounding unincorporated County areas of Stevenson Ranch and Castaic"; "District No. 26, formed in 1962, served the eastern half of the Valley while District No. 32, formed in 1965, served the western half"; "A formal agreement was signed between the two Districts in 1984"; "In 2005 ... the two Districts were consolidated, and the Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District was born"; "governed by a Board of Directors consisting of the Mayor of Santa Clarita, a second city council member from Santa Clarita, and the Chairperson of the County Board of Supervisors"; "250,000 residents and businesses"; "over 42 miles of trunk sewers, one pumping plant, and two sewage treatment plants"; "local sewers and laterals that connect to the Districts' trunk sewers ... are the responsibility of the local jurisdictions"; "a confederation of 24 independent special districts" formed under "the County Sanitation District Act of 1923".

Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Saugus Water Reclamation Plant," https://www.lacsd.org/services/wastewater-sewage/facilities/saugus-water-reclamation-plant, as captured by the Internet Archive on 19 May 2026: "Saugus WRP began operation in 1962. Plant expansion occurred in 1964, 1965, and 1968. The plant was upgraded to tertiary level of treatment with the addition of dual media pressure filters in 1987. The addition of flow equalization facilities in 1991 brought the plant to its current design capacity of 6.5 MGD"; "No facilities for solids processing are located at the Saugus WRP."

Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Valencia Water Reclamation Plant," https://www.lacsd.org/services/wastewater-sewage/facilities/valencia-water-reclamation-plant, as captured by the Internet Archive on 18 February 2026: "The Valencia WRP occupies 27 acres west of the Golden State (I-5) Freeway. The treatment plant was placed in operation in 1967, and initially had a capacity of 1.5 million gallons per day"; "completed in May 2003 for a final design capacity of 21.6 MGD"; "processes all wastewater solids generated in the Santa Clarita Valley Sanitation District."

Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Chloride in Santa Clarita: Frequently Asked Questions," http://www.lacsd.org/info/industrial_waste/chloride_in_santa_clarita/frequently_asked_questions.asp, as captured by the Internet Archive on 12 March 2012: "Measure S approved by voters on November 4, 2008, enacted the Santa Clara River Chloride Reduction Ordinance of 2008. The ordinance required the removal of all residential automatic water softeners by June 30, 2009"; "The Los Angeles Regional Water Quality Control Board (Regional Board) has set a water quality objective of 100 milligrams per liter for the Santa Clara River"; the plants "are not designed to remove chloride."

Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Santa Clarita Chloride Compliance," https://www.lacsd.org/services/wastewater-programs-permits/santa-clarita-chloride-compliance, as captured by the Internet Archive on 14 January 2026: "In October 2013, the SCVSD Board of Directors approved a project to comply with the State-mandated chloride limit and certified the associated Environmental Impact Report"; "The Court, nonetheless, set aside the 2013 EIR"; "On August 30, 2017, the SCVSD Board of Directors certified the Final Recirculated EIR"; "on February 16, 2022, denied a petition from the challenger for rehearing. This effectively ended the lawsuit"; "start-up in July 2021 at the Saugus WRP and August 2021 at the Valencia WRP"; "Construction of the AWT at the Valencia WRP began in April 2019 with start-up in October 2023"; brine trucked to "the Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts' A.K. Warren Water Resource Recovery Facility in Carson."

Los Angeles County Sanitation Districts, "Automatic Water Softeners," https://www.lacsd.org/wastewater/automatic_water_softeners/default.asp, as captured by the Internet Archive on 14 December 2018: "These efforts have resulted in the removal of over 8,000 salt discharging automatic water softeners and significant reductions in chloride levels."

editorNotes.heading: Two dates for the ultraviolet start-up at Valencia
editorNotes.note: The Districts' chloride compliance page gives August 2021 for the start of ultraviolet disinfection at the Valencia plant; the Valencia plant's own page gives July 2021. The body says 2021.

title: Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning
body:
The Department of Regional Planning is the County's planning department for every part of Los Angeles County outside a city, and so for Castaic, Stevenson Ranch, Val Verde, Agua Dulce and the rest of the unincorporated valley. It writes the long-range plans, reviews development projects and answers zoning complaints.[1][2] It began as the staff of the Regional Planning Commission, founded in 1923, and became an independent County department in 1974.[1]

Its plan for the valley is the Santa Clarita Valley Area Plan, a part of the County General Plan that applies only to the unincorporated valley. The Board of Supervisors adopted it on November 27, 2012, and it took effect on December 27. It is the County's half of "One Valley One Vision," a joint planning effort with the City of Santa Clarita, whose General Plan, the other half, the City Council had adopted on June 14, 2011.[3] It replaced the County's area plan of 1984, revised in 1990.[4][5] The department is the lead agency for the environmental review of the County's projects in the valley, as for the NorthLake Specific Plan near Castaic in 2017 and Tesoro del Valle in 2018.[6][5]
footnotes: Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, "About Us," https://planning.lacounty.gov/about-us/, read 5 October 2026: "LA County Planning started with the founding of the Los Angeles County Regional Planning Commission in 1923. We provided staff advice and help to the Commission. In 1974, we became an independent County Department"; "LA County Planning is the planning department for all areas outside a city in LA County"; "We help write long range plans, review development projects, and respond to zoning complaints."

County of Los Angeles, Fifth Supervisorial District, Guide to Unincorporated Area Services, 2024, https://lacounty.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/SD5-English-Guide-to-Unincorporated-Area-Services-1-1.pdf: lists among the district's unincorporated areas Acton, Agua Dulce, Castaic, Stevenson Ranch and Val Verde.

Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, "Santa Clarita Valley Area Plan," https://planning.lacounty.gov/long-range-planning/santa-clarita-valley-area-plan/, read 5 October 2026: "adopted by the County Board of Supervisors on November 27, 2012 and took effect on December 27, 2012"; "apply only to the unincorporated portions of the Santa Clarita Valley"; "a component of 'One Valley One Vision', a joint planning effort with the City of Santa Clarita. The other component is the City of Santa Clarita General Plan, which was adopted by the Santa Clarita City Council on June 14, 2011."

Leon Worden, note on "OVOV City-County General Plan: Cultural Resources, Santa Clarita Valley," SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/laco_ovov_final_2010.htm: "OVOV wholly replaces the city's 1991 General Plan and the county's Santa Clarita Valley Area Plan of 1984 as revised in 1990."

Tesoro del Valle Phases A, B, C, Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Report, February 2018, lead agency County of Los Angeles Department of Regional Planning, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/tesoro_sdeir0218.htm, flipbook page 171: "the Santa Clarita Valley Area Plan (1990 SCVAP), (adopted in 1984 comprehensively updated in 1990, amended in 2007)"; "repealed by the BOS and replaced with the current SCVAP in 2012."

NorthLake Specific Plan Project, Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Report, May 2017, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/northlakehills_deir_0517.htm, title page: "Lead Agency: County of Los Angeles Department of Regional Planning."

editorNotes.heading: A second date for the County's adoption
editorNotes.note: The note on the archive's page for the One Valley One Vision cultural resources section says the Board of Supervisors adopted the plan on February 28, 2012. The County's own page gives November 27, 2012, with effect from December 27, 2012, and the body follows the County.

title: Los Angeles County Regional Planning Commission
body:
The Regional Planning Commission is the Board of Supervisors' advisory body on planning for the unincorporated county, the unincorporated Santa Clarita Valley among it. Its five commissioners are appointed by the Board to four-year terms; they hold public hearings and administer the State Planning Law, the Subdivision Map Act, the California Environmental Quality Act and the County's zoning and subdivision ordinances.[1] It was founded in 1923, and the County's planning department grew out of its staff.[2]

Its hearings have shaped much of the valley outside the city. In October 1964 it heard the zone change for Princess Park Estates in the Valencia Valley, where slides early in 1969 forced the demolition of a number of homes.[3] It recommended to the Board the plan amendment for Skyline Ranch in Canyon Country, whose environmental report the Board certified on December 7, 2010.[4] In 2005 applicants for land-use permits in Agua Dulce told the Superior Court that County staff, the Commission or the Board had sent them to present their projects to the Agua Dulce Town Council before the County would consider them further.[5]
footnotes: Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, "Regional Planning Commission," https://planning.lacounty.gov/public-hearings-and-meetings/regional-planning-commission/, read 5 October 2026: "acts as an advisory body to the County Board of Supervisors on all planning matters. They administer provisions of the State Planning Law ..., the State Subdivision Map Act, California Environmental Quality Act, and the LA County ordinances affecting planning such as the County Zoning Ordinance and Subdivision Ordinance"; "RPC consists of five Commissioners. They are appointed to four-year terms by the County Board of Supervisors."

Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning, "About Us," https://planning.lacounty.gov/about-us/, read 5 October 2026: "LA County Planning started with the founding of the Los Angeles County Regional Planning Commission in 1923."

Ken Gosting, "Sliding Disasters: More Ahead," part II of four, The Newhall Signal and Saugus Enterprise, March 1969 (part I appeared Wednesday, March 26, 1969), as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sg19650916.htm: "Members of the Regional Planning Commission after hearing Zoning Case No. 4833 on October 13, 1964, were certain Princess Park would set an example for many other developers to follow"; "the sliding problems which caused the demolition of a number of Valencia Valley homes last month."

County of Los Angeles Department of Regional Planning, Skyline Ranch approval package, November 13, 2017, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/skylineranch111317.htm: flipbook page 28, "A RESOLUTION OF THE REGIONAL PLANNING COMMISSION OF THE COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES RELATING TO PROJECT NO. 04-075-(5) GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT CASE NO. 200900009"; page 37, "the Regional Planning Commission of the County of Los Angeles recommends that the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors: 1. Hold a public hearing to consider the above recommended general plan amendment"; page 21, "The final EIR certified by the Board of Supervisors on December 7, 2010."

Johnson et al. v. Agua Dulce Town Council, Los Angeles County Superior Court No. BS 096594, judgment of August 1, 2005, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/aguadulcetowncouncil080105.htm, finding 11: "These applicants report that Los Angeles County staff or the Los Angeles Regional Planning Commission or the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors has directed them to present their projects to Respondent and to seek Respondent's support. The applicants report, further, that the County would not consider their applications further until after they had presented their projects to Respondent."

title: Castaic Area Town Council
body:
The Castaic Area Town Council is a nonprofit corporation whose ten directors are elected by Castaic's residents, two from each of five regions, to speak for the unincorporated community to the County. It reviews land-use applications and other proposals before County Planning and works with the Board of Supervisors and County departments such as Regional Planning and Parks and Recreation.[1][2] It is not a government. Its bylaws make it "a voluntary organization of elected members who receive no remuneration," bar it from borrowing, and give its purposes as presenting "community concerns to appropriate agencies" and reviewing "public or private proposals that may affect the community."[1] The Internal Revenue Service lists it as a 501(c)(3) organization, recognized in 2001.[3]

Its bylaws were adopted on July 19, 2000. They set its area as that of the Castaic Union School District, with the Peter Pitchess Honor Rancho east of Castaic Creek, and its directors' terms at four years, no more than two in a row. A director must be an adult, a registered voter, and a resident of his or her region for a year; elections were set for the first Tuesday in November, by secret ballot under an election committee.[1] Half its seats are now filled every two years.[2] The County treats it as the community's voice: its notice for the Tapia Ranch project of 2007 lists the "Castaic Town Council" among the special reviewing agencies.[4]
footnotes: Bylaws of Castaic Area Town Council Inc., adopted July 19, 2000, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/catcbylaws07192000.pdf: "A California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation"; "To present community concerns to appropriate agencies, to review public or private proposals that may affect the community"; "shall at all times function as a voluntary organization of elected members who receive no remuneration"; "shall not borrow money nor incur indebtedness"; "the area within the current boundaries of the Castaic Union School District, including The Peter Pitchess Honor Rancho east of Castaic Creek"; "composed of ten directors elected by the Castaic Area resident. Two directors shall be elected from each Region"; "a resident of minimum one year and a registered voter"; "shall serve for a term of four years. No one may serve continuously for more than two full elected terms"; "There shall be an election on the first Tuesday in the month of November"; "The election shall be by secret ballot on ballots prepared by the Election Committee"; "ADOPTED: Date: July 19, 2000."

Castaic Area Town Council, home page, https://www.castaictowncouncil.org/, read 5 October 2026: "The town council is a non-profit 501c3 volunteer advisory board representing the community of Castaic working alongside the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors and various County Departments such as Public Safety, Regional Planning, and Parks & Recreation. The Castaic Area Town Council is comprised of 10 (ten) elected representatives from 5 (five) regions, within unincorporated Castaic. Elections are held every 2 (two) years, with a 4 (four) year commitment"; its Land Use Committee posts proposals before "Los Angeles County Planning."

Internal Revenue Service exempt-organization data for Castaic Area Town Council Inc, EIN 95-4809070, as published by ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/api/v2/organizations/954809070.json, read 5 October 2026: subsection 3, ruling date April 2001.

Tapia Ranch Development, Notice of Preparation and Initial Study, County of Los Angeles, 2007, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/tapiaranch_nop_20070829.htm, flipbook page 17, "Reviewing Agencies": "Castaic Town Council" listed in the column of special reviewing agencies with the Castaic Union School District, the City of Santa Clarita and the Castaic Lake Water Agency.

editorNotes.heading: When it was founded
editorNotes.note: The bylaws of July 19, 2000 are the earliest document found that names the council; whether it existed before them is not known.

openQuestions: orgLevel: a town council is not a level of government; left empty. Nathan's call whether "valley" is wanted for /civic grouping.
Founding date: not found before the 2000 bylaws. A contemporary Signal report of its formation would settle it.

Whether the Brown Act binds it is left out of the body: Darryl Manzer's commentary of August 2, 2014 on SCVNews.com says it does, but that is an opinion column, not a ruling. The 2005 Agua Dulce judgment rests on a charter adopted by the town's voters; whether Castaic has one is not known.

title: Agua Dulce Town Council
body:
The Agua Dulce Town Council speaks for Agua Dulce, an unincorporated town, to the County and other governments. Its seven members are elected by Agua Dulce's registered voters to two-year terms, in an election each November run by its own election committee. It reviews public and private proposals that may affect the community and gives the County its recommendation on land-use applications there.[1][2][3] It cannot make law: its bylaws say it "cannot pass laws, and cannot levy assessments or taxes," and that its charter gives it no authority over anyone except that it "is the only group that can speak for the community."[2] The Internal Revenue Service lists it as a 501(c)(4) organization.[4]

Agua Dulce's residents created it by approving its charter on September 21, 1991, and it was incorporated as a nonprofit public benefit corporation in 1994.[1][3] In April 2005 it voted that its meetings were not to be recorded by outsiders, and residents sued. Ruling on August 1, 2005, the Superior Court held that the unincorporated town is a "local agency" under the Brown Act and the council, created by charter and serving "in an advisory capacity to the community of Agua Dulce and to the County of Los Angeles," a legislative body bound by it. The council had rescinded the ban in May, so the case was dismissed.[3] The court recorded applicants' testimony that County staff, the Regional Planning Commission or the Board of Supervisors had sent them to the council first.[3] With the Acton Town Council it opposed the Cemex sand and gravel mine in Soledad Canyon, and when the Board of Supervisors approved the mine's permit in 2004 the two councils were each given a seat on its community advisory committee.[5]
footnotes: Charter for Agua Dulce Town Council, "Approved and Adopted September 21, 1991," https://adtowncouncil.com/pdf/ADTC2005CharterPDF.pdf, read 5 October 2026: "This Charter creates an Agua Dulce Town Council"; "To review public and private proposals that may affect the community"; "The Town Council shall consist of seven (7) members elected by the registered voters of Agua Dulce."

Agua Dulce Town Council Bylaws and Election Procedures, amended June 8, 2022, https://adtowncouncil.com/pdf/ADTCBylawsElectionProcedures6-8-22.pdf, read 5 October 2026: "The CHARTER does not impart any authority to the Council over any person or group with the exception that the Council is the only group that can speak for the community"; "The Council cannot pass laws, and cannot levy assessments or taxes"; "Council elections shall be held each year in November on Election Day"; "all Council members shall be elected to serve for two (2) years."

Johnson et al. v. Agua Dulce Town Council, Los Angeles County Superior Court No. BS 096594, judgment of August 1, 2005, Dzintra Janavs, judge, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/aguadulcetowncouncil080105.htm: "Respondent, the Agua Dulce Town Council was created in 1991 by the approval and adoption, by the residents of Agua Dulce ... of the 'Charter for Agua Dulce Town Council'. Respondent is an active California non-profit public benefit corporation, incorporated in 1994"; "On April 27, 2005, Respondent passed a motion that 'Agua Dulce Town Council meetings are not to be electronically recorded by any outside entity or entities'"; "On May 18, 2005 ... Respondent passed a motion rescinding"; "Respondent is a 'legislative body' ... in that it serves in an advisory capacity to the community of Agua Dulce and to the County of Los Angeles, and was created by a Charter"; finding 11 on applicants directed to the council.

Agua Dulce Town Council, home page, https://adtowncouncil.com/, read 5 October 2026: "a California nonprofit organization and exempt from Federal income tax under section 501(c)4 of the Internal Revenue Code." Internal Revenue Service exempt-organization data, EIN 95-4491719, as published by ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, read 5 October 2026: subsection 4, ruling date August 2010.

County of Los Angeles, Surface Mining Permit No. 91-165-(5), Cemex, Inc., Board of Supervisors, June 2, 2004, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/laco_cemexpermit060204.htm: flipbook page 4, at the hearing of January 23, 2001 the Board "requested that County staff, Cemex, and representatives of Santa Clarita and the Acton and Aqua Dulce Town Councils meet"; page 80, "the Project opponents (the City and the Agua Dulce and Acton Town councils)"; page 250, the community advisory committee to include "Agua Dulce Town Council (1) Acton Town Council (1)."

editorNotes.heading: The charter's date
editorNotes.note: The charter is published as a file named for 2005 but carries the heading "Approved and Adopted September 21, 1991"; it may have been amended since. The bylaws and the 2005 judgment both give 1991.

title: Acton Town Council
body:
The Acton Town Council is an elected advisory council for the unincorporated town of Acton. Its members, up to seven, are elected to two-year terms in an annual November election by the registered voters of Acton as the Acton Community Standards District bounds it, and serve without pay. It gathers the community's views, presents its concerns to the agencies concerned, and reviews public and private proposals that may affect the town.[1][2] In law it is a limited liability company, The Acton Town Council, LLC, whose sole member is "The Town of Acton Advisory Board," that is, the seated council members; the Internal Revenue Service lists it as a 501(c)(4) organization.[1][3]

Its bylaws date its second election to 1990.[1] It opposed the Cemex sand and gravel mine in Soledad Canyon with the Agua Dulce Town Council and the City of Santa Clarita, and when the Board of Supervisors approved the mine's permit in 2004 it was given a seat on the mine's community advisory committee.[4]
footnotes: The Acton Town Council, LLC, Bylaws, "Revised and approved 04/07/2025," https://actontowncouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Bylaws_Final_Revision_04_07_2025.pdf, read 5 October 2026: "The LLC which is held by one sole member, The Town of Acton Advisory Board"; "recognized by the federal government and the State of CA as a 501(c) 4 non-profit"; "To present community concerns to appropriate agencies, and To review public or private proposals which may affect the community"; "Function as a voluntary organization of elected members who receive no remuneration"; "a maximum of seven (7) elected members"; "a registered voter within the unincorporated area of Acton as defined by the Acton Community Standards District"; "Members of the Council shall serve for a term of two years"; "an annual election, in November"; "The second election of the Council (1990)."

Acton Town Council, "2026 Acton Town Council Election, Tuesday, November 3rd," July 31, 2026, https://actontowncouncil.org/2026/07/2026-acton-town-council-election-tuesday-november-3rd/: "Each seat is for a 2-year term"; candidates "must be a resident and a registered voter in the unincorporated area of Acton."

Internal Revenue Service exempt-organization data for Acton Town Council LLC, EIN 81-3712497, as published by ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/api/v2/organizations/813712497.json, read 5 October 2026: subsection 4, ruling date June 2017.

County of Los Angeles, Surface Mining Permit No. 91-165-(5), Cemex, Inc., Board of Supervisors, June 2, 2004, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/laco_cemexpermit060204.htm: flipbook page 80, "the Project opponents (the City and the Agua Dulce and Acton Town councils)"; page 250, "Acton Town Council (1)."

editorNotes.heading: Founding
editorNotes.note: The bylaws give 1990 as the year of the council's second election, which puts its first in or about 1989; no document of its founding was found.

openQuestions: Acton is in the Antelope Valley, not the Santa Clarita Valley; it is proposed because the archive covers Acton and its school district is on /civic. Nathan's call.
Members in the archive's obituaries (Lawrence H. Layton, /scvhistory/obituary_lawrencehoyttlayton.htm; Ray F. Billet) have no person records; no holdings proposed.

title: Val Verde Civic Association
body:
The Val Verde Civic Association is an association of Val Verde residents and a nonprofit organization, which the Internal Revenue Service lists as a 501(c)(4) organization recognized in 1990.[1] It is not a town council of the kind Agua Dulce and Castaic elect. Darryl Manzer wrote in 2014 that it is neither appointed nor elected through a County process, and that the County's advisory body for Val Verde is a separate committee whose members the Fifth District supervisor appoints.[2]

When the Samuel Dixon health clinic in Val Verde closed for lack of funds in 1990, the association campaigned to save it with Jo Anne Darcy, deputy to Supervisor Michael D. Antonovich, and won a County community block grant that reopened it; it was rededicated in February 1991.[3] In February 1997 it and Citizens Against Chiquita signed with the Newhall Land and Farming Company and Laidlaw Waste Systems (Chiquita) a statement of agreements and understandings on the expansion of the Chiquita Canyon Landfill, by which the landfill funded community benefits in Val Verde in exchange for the groups' non-opposition.[4] It gave Miriam Canty a special award for her work with Val Verde's young people.[5]
footnotes: Internal Revenue Service exempt-organization data for Val Verde Civic Association, EIN 95-4269196, as published by ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/api/v2/organizations/954269196.json, read 5 October 2026: subsection 4, ruling date October 1990.

Darryl Manzer, "Thumbs Up or Down," commentary, SCVNews.com, August 2, 2014, https://scvnews.com/thumbs-up-or-down-commentary-by-darryl-manzer: "The Val Verde Civic Association is not appointed or elected through a county-used process. It is an association of private citizens who live in Val Verde"; "The members of the Val Verde Community Advisory Committee (VVCAC) are appointed by 'the member of the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors representing the Fifth District.'"

Miriam Canty, "History of the Samuel Dixon Family Health Center," November 2000, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/samdixon-miriamcanty.htm: "The center was briefly closed in 1990 due to lack of funds"; "The Val Verde Civic Association, faced with losing the health clinic, mounted a community awareness campaign with the assistance of Jo Anne Darcy, deputy to Supervisor Michael D. Antonovich. They obtained a community block grant from the county to re-open the clinic. In February 1991, during the rededication ceremony."

Chiquita Canyon Landfill Expansion and Related Facilities Project 389-081, Statement of Agreements and Understandings By and Between Newhall Land and Farming Co., Laidlaw Waste Systems (Chiquita) Inc., Val Verde Civic Association (and Citizens Against Chiquita), executed February 1997, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/chiquita-valverde1997.htm, with Leon Worden's summary: "22-year funding agreement ($250,000 minimum, annually) for community benefits in Val Verde in exchange for non-opposition to the expansion of the Chiquita Canyon Landfill, 1997."

"Miriam Canty, Val Verde Leader, 1916-2001," obituary, The Signal, as carried on SCVHistory.com, /scvhistory/sg022101b.htm: "She received a special award from the Val Verde Civic Association for her work with the youth of the community."

editorNotes.heading: Whose judgment
